body_markdown:
This was never going to be a small project. Once I decided that my Boxster, which I’ve had for 12 years, was going to get a major service, including the clutch, IMS bearing, and valve chain guides, I knew I’d be in for a penny, in for a pound. Or several pounds, as it ended up.


I was prepared for this eventuality, even if, when I got started, I didn’t know what I’d be spending those additional pennies on. Some items were part of logical tune-ups; others were effects of the “while-I’m-in-there” syndrome that seems to be congenital among car folk. Once things are apart, systems and components are often temptingly exposed and accessible.


As I shared in the first installment of *[Bringing Boxster Back](https://www.hagerty.com/media/our-garage/bringing-boxster-back-1-eyes-wide-open/)* , my goal was to get this car sorted for the long term, and knocking it out in one go appealed to me more than drawing out the work over several years, repeating disassembly over and over. Don’t get me wrong, wrenching does bring me peace, but real peace also comes from knowing a car has no needs.


With that, these are the while-you’re-in-there’s I’d recommend any first-gen Boxster owner consider when laying their car up for service. Note that I bought everything myself; any shoutouts to brands are because I am pleased with their product. Subsequent columns will cover more fun and sparkly bits, so lest you think I’ve forgotten about suspension or exhaust or anything else, stay tuned.


## The Basics


The view from your Boxster engine’s window.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


Yoinking the engine out from under the Boxster may have been slight overkill. It *is* , however, a lot easier to access the timing chain guides that way. And since a shop, Steinel’s Autowerks, was doing that as well as installing a solution to this car’s infamous intermediate shaft (IMS) bearing flaw, I figured I’d save a few bucks on labor by dropping off the engine myself. Besides, I was eager to[put my new lift to good use](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/4-things-to-consider-when-buying-a-lift-for-your-garage/) .


Fresh dual-mass flywheel and clutch going in.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


Not too oily behind the flywheel…


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


…but all cleaned up now, and no more IMS uncertainty.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


Sitting at 77,000-ish miles, the 3.2-liter flat-six in my Boxster had its 60K-mile service about a decade ago. It was time, once again, for the basics, as well as some other important bits. Out back, the rear main seal was a must-do, and since the clutch and flywheel were coming off, it was also a no-brainer. Further up the rear of the engine sits the air-oil separator. When this fails, it can allow a lot of oil into the intake, creating a white puff of smoke on startup and causing more rapid oil consumption. Steinel’s recommends the OEM part in this instance.


Fresh coolant hoses and a new serpentine belt went onto the front of the engine. The latter is a simple change with the engine installed, but it was due, so I went ahead. It’s also worth noting that if you’ve dumped the coolant, replacing other hoses by the radiators isn’t a bad idea, either.


Working my way from left (new coil design) to right.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


For spark, I replaced the plugs, spark plug tubes (the O-rings on said tubes are the critical part here, but the tubes themselves can also fail), and coils. The original coils are prone to cracking, so it’s worth pursuing the revised part (99760210704) for these.


## Drivetrain Mounts… Best to Tackle All Three


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


On the last several drives before I took it all apart, I noticed a bit of additional vibration, especially when transitioning on and off throttle. The engine mount seemed the likely culprit, and as you can see above, the original on the left was all kinds of cracked. You can buy a replacement center section and press it in to save a few bucks, but I went with a more standard complete part. Note that this job, as well as the transmission mounts, is easy to do with the drivetrain in the car, too, as long as you support the engine properly.


Ye olde fluid-filled mount.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


The simple PRG Products 986 transmission mount.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


It wasn’t until I had everything buttoned up that I discovered the error of my ways in not changing the transmission mounts at the same time. The shifter balked at going into gear on occasion, something it hadn’t done in the past. Internet-aided diagnosis of 986 transmission issues can be a bit like looking up why your eye is a little itchy, only to read health websites that say you’re going to die tomorrow. It *could* be that bad, but odds are it’s not, and there’s an easy fix. I questioned myself momentarily because these transmissions are evidently sensitive to fluid type as well as fill level… but I used the OEM-style oil and was careful in loading it up.


I examined the original, fluid-filled mounts and they didn’t look so hot. Because the Porsche part was an arm and a leg, I went on the hunt for solutions. Turns out 993 mounts are a cheaper OEM fix (who knew air-cooled 911 parts would be less expensive than their lowly Boxster equivalents?), and there’s a healthy aftermarket selection of them. I went with solid urethane mounts from PRG Products: They aren’t a full-on race durometer bushing (good for this road car, then), are simpler in construction than the originals, and I don’t feel any difference in vibration from working stock parts. All for less money. These, as well as hitting the transmission’s external shift levers with a healthy amount of silicone lubricant, solved my shifting problems.


## Don’t Crack Under Pressure


Coolant expansion tank: This one is easy-peasy if the engine’s out, and probably not too bad with just the transmission out, but I could see how it’d generate some four-letter words if done on its own. For me, it was a high-priority “while you’re in there” choice.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


The tanks are known for cracking at the split between the clear and the black plastic, and it’s a good idea to quickly inspect it by pulling up your trunk carpet and checking for moisture. Mine was slightly damp, and I caught the faintest whiff of coolant, so while I didn’t see an obvious crack, it probably wouldn’t have been long before I had a real problem.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


There’s nothing particularly difficult about the expansion tank install itself; it’s getting access to the hose connections on the engine side of the trunk wall that can be an issue. Also, this is one of those times when you buy the Porsche-branded part—there are many reports online of cheaper alternatives either weeping between the two types of plastic, or the three nipples (shown below) having insufficient cooling flow because of incomplete drilling during manufacturing. Be sure to inspect your new tank before installation. Finally, toss in a new coolant cap for good measure—the updated part number is 99610644704.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


## An Unlikely Addition


This typically isn’t a “while you’re in there” job, but if you don’t know whether your fuel pump’s been replaced (remember, these cars are at least 22 years old at this point), I suggest you consider it the next time your Boxster is parked for service. Is this overkill? Maybe. But do you want to go on a long road trip and have to get towed or fix the car on the side of the road because your quarter-century-old fuel pump failed? No, no, you do not.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


Last June, the Hagerty Media team got together for our annual group drive. The intent was to bring my Boxster, my dad’s C5 Corvette, and my colleague Eric Weiner’s BMW Z3 together for an early 2000s convertible showdown. The day before the trip, I went to move the Boxster and it cranked to life, sputtered, then died. Confirming it wasn’t the relay meant that it was the fuel pump itself. So much for team fun with the Boxster, but I was glad it happened in my barn rather than on the road.


Having broken a plastic fuel pump ring nut before, I splurged for a proper tool.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


Before we get to the pump, it’s a good idea to buy a fuel pump relay. These aren’t available at local parts stores, and they’re anywhere from about $15 (aftermarket) to $40 (Porsche) online. Even though mine was fine, I bought a spare and tucked it in the pouch of my spare tire just in case.


It was all filled up, so I pumped out a little more than 15 gallons.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


As for the pump itself, it’s a pretty straightforward fix, but because it’s locked into a ring on the bottom of the tank, it’s prudent to get rid of whatever fuel’s in there first. Be sure to do this in a well-ventilated area, and obviously make sure nothing that can spark is nearby. One thing to note: The float for the gas gauge can get hung up on the lines for the pump, so make sure it has full range of motion before you button things up.


What’d I miss? I’ve been pleasantly surprised to see so many Boxster fans come out of the woodwork, commenting effusively on the couple of pieces I’ve written about the car so far. Keep the notes coming! Up next: Everything in the wheel wells.
